name: The Oort Cloud
statement: Far beyond the planets, a vast shell of icy bodies wraps the Sun and feeds long comets.
statementAccent: a vast shell of icy bodies wraps the Sun
meaning: The Oort cloud is a vast, roughly spherical shell of icy bodies hypothesized to surround the Sun at enormous distances, far beyond the planets and the Kuiper Belt. Composed of billions of cometary nuclei, it is thought to be the reservoir from which long-period comets originate. The cloud is believed to stretch from a few thousand astronomical units out to perhaps a hundred thousand astronomical units or more, extending a good fraction of the way to the nearest star. It is usually divided into a disk-shaped inner region, the Hills cloud, and a spherical outer region. Because long-period comets arrive from all directions, the source that feeds them must enclose the solar system as a sphere, which is the central evidence for the cloud's existence. Named after the Dutch astronomer Jan Oort, who proposed it in 1950, with an earlier related idea from Ernst Öpik, the Oort cloud remains hypothetical, inferred from comets rather than directly observed, since no telescope can yet see its distant, dim members in place.
mechanism: The Oort cloud is thought to have formed from icy planetesimals that first coalesced much closer to the Sun, among the giant planets, and were then flung outward by gravitational encounters with those planets into enormously wide, loosely bound orbits. At such great distances the Sun's grip is weak, so the bodies are vulnerable to gentle perturbations from passing stars, from the tidal pull of the galaxy itself, and from giant molecular clouds. These perturbations can nudge an Oort cloud object out of its remote orbit and send it plunging toward the inner solar system, where it appears as a long-period comet on a long, often nearly parabolic orbit that can take thousands or millions of years. The spherical shape of the outer cloud explains why such comets come from every direction, unlike the planets and Kuiper Belt objects that lie near the ecliptic plane. The inner Hills cloud, more disk-like and denser, is thought to resupply the outer cloud over time, sustaining the reservoir of comets.

examples.text: Long-period comets on very long, randomly oriented orbits are thought to be Oort cloud objects nudged inward toward the Sun.
Because long-period comets arrive from every direction, their source must be a spherical shell enclosing the solar system, not a flat disk.
Passing stars and the tidal pull of the galaxy can dislodge Oort cloud bodies, sending them sunward as comets.

variants.name: The inner Hills cloud
variants.text: The denser, disk-shaped inner region of the cloud, thought to resupply the spherical outer cloud over time.

variants.name: The outer Oort cloud
variants.text: The spherical outer region, weakly bound and susceptible to perturbations that send its bodies inward as long-period comets.

whyItMatters: The Oort cloud is a cornerstone concept in understanding the outer solar system and the origin of comets. It provides the reservoir that explains where long-period comets come from and why they arrive from all directions on enormously long orbits, tying the occasional appearance of a bright comet to the vast, unseen edge of the Sun's domain. As a relic of the solar system's formation, populated by material flung out by the young giant planets, the cloud preserves pristine icy bodies that carry clues to the conditions of the early solar system. Its outer reaches mark the boundary of the Sun's gravitational influence, extending a good fraction of the way to neighbouring stars, and its bodies are sensitive to the galactic environment, linking the solar system to the wider galaxy. Although still hypothetical and beyond the reach of direct observation, the Oort cloud is essential to models of the solar system's structure, history, and connection to interstellar space.

working.text: have the young giant planets scatter icy planetesimals into enormously wide, loosely bound orbits around the Sun.
let these bodies settle into a vast spherical outer cloud and a denser disk-like inner Hills cloud far beyond the planets.
let perturbations from passing stars and the galaxy nudge bodies inward, where they appear as long-period comets.

limits: The Oort cloud is hypothetical and inferred, not directly observed, since present telescopes cannot detect its distant, faint members in place; the evidence is indirect, drawn chiefly from the orbits of long-period comets. Its dimensions are uncertain and model-dependent, with the outer edge variously placed near a hundred thousand or up to two hundred thousand astronomical units, so specific distances should be treated as estimates rather than measured facts. The division into inner Hills cloud and outer cloud and the details of its formation and replenishment are theoretical reconstructions. Even the total mass and number of bodies are poorly constrained. So the Oort cloud is a well-motivated and widely accepted hypothesis that explains long-period comets and the edge of the solar system, understood as inferred structure whose precise size, shape, and content remain uncertain.
misreadings: The Oort cloud has never been directly seen; it is inferred from comets, so it is a strong hypothesis rather than an observed object, and its exact size is uncertain and model-dependent. It is not the same as the Kuiper Belt, which is a nearer, flatter disk beyond Neptune, whereas the Oort cloud is a far more distant spherical shell. And it is not a dense, crowded region, since its bodies are spread across an enormous volume, so treating the Oort cloud as directly observed, as identical to the Kuiper Belt, or as densely packed, misreads a vast, tenuous, inferred reservoir of comets at the edge of the Sun's reach.
origin: Proposed by the Dutch astronomer Jan Oort in 1950, building on an earlier idea by Ernst Öpik; a hypothetical spherical shell of icy bodies at the far edge of the solar system, the source of long-period comets.
